summaries.example: Imagine a class chart. Each student has a quiz score and a result: pass or try again. If every student with the same score always gets the same result, then the result depends on the score. A dependence atom is a special logic statement that records this pattern.
summaries.summary: Dependence logic is a new version of first-order logic. It lets us say clearly when one value is determined by other values. For example, we can say that a result depends only on a score, or that one choice depends on two earlier choices. This is useful because the order of ordinary quantifiers cannot show every possible pattern. Dependence logic uses teams, which are sets of assignments. An assignment gives values to variables; a team collects several assignments together. A formula is judged against the whole team. For ordinary first-order formulas, this agrees with the usual method: every assignment in the team must satisfy the formula. Dependence atoms add the important new idea. If two assignments agree on the values that determine y, they must also agree on y. The logic also has a game interpretation. One player tries to show that a statement is true, but choices must be uniform: the same determining information must lead to the same dependent value. Dependence logic has connections with databases, belief states, voting, computer science, and ways of describing causes or counterfactual changes.
key_ideas: Ordinary first-order logic can show some patterns of dependence through the order of its quantifiers.
Dependence logic adds dependence atoms so it can describe more complicated patterns directly.
In team semantics, a team is a group of possible ways things might be.
A game version of the idea uses strategies, but a strategy must follow the stated dependence rules.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dependence logic gives a careful language for talking about information and determination. The same pattern appears when a database field is fixed by another field, when a decision follows from available information, or when a choice must be made without seeing certain facts. It also shows that changing how we define truth can help logic describe relationships that ordinary sentence-by-sentence methods do not express easily.

important_terms.definition: A way to study whether one value is fixed by, or determined by, other values.
A logic statement saying that one variable’s value is determined by the values of other variables.
A set of possible assignments, where each assignment gives values to variables.
A way of deciding whether a formula is true by looking at a whole team instead of one assignment at a time.

questions_to_think_about: Can a result depend on two pieces of information together even when it does not depend on either one alone?
Why might it be useful to study a group of possibilities instead of just one possibility?
What would happen if two students had the same score but different results?

summaries.example: Suppose a selection process assigns each applicant a label y from two recorded features x1 and x2. The claim that y depends on both features says: whenever two possible records agree on x1 and x2, they must agree on y. It does not say that y depends on x1 alone. A team containing records (0,0,0), (0,1,1), (1,0,1), and (1,1,2) satisfies dependence on x1 and x2, but not dependence on x1 alone.
summaries.summary: Dependence logic extends first-order logic with dependence atoms, written schematically as =(x1,...,xn,y). Such an atom says that y is functionally determined by x1 through xn: across a team, any two assignments agreeing on the determining variables must agree on y. This differs from independence-friendly and branching quantifier approaches, which encode unusual dependencies through quantifier structure itself. Dependence logic instead states the dependency as a separate condition. Its main semantics is team semantics. A team is a set of assignments, and satisfaction is defined for the set as a whole. First-order literals must hold in every assignment, conjunction requires both conjuncts to hold, universal quantification expands each assignment through all possible values, and existential quantification adds one or more permitted values. Disjunction divides the team into subteams that satisfy the two alternatives. These rules yield locality, downward closure, and the empty-team property. For sentences, truth can be defined using a team containing only the empty assignment. There is also a game-theoretic semantics: a player seeks a winning strategy, but the strategy must be uniform at dependence atoms, so equal determining information cannot produce different dependent choices. This game account agrees with team semantics. At the sentence level, dependence logic matches existential second-order logic in expressive power. At the formula level, however, the class of definable teams is constrained by downward closure. The entry also surveys variants such as independence logic, inclusion logic, team logic, modal and propositional forms, temporal team semantics, and quantitative versions. key_ideas: Quantifier nesting in first-order logic creates dependency patterns, but those patterns are necessarily ordered and transitive.
Dependence atoms separate the statement of a dependency from the quantifiers that introduce variables.
Team semantics generalizes ordinary semantics: for first-order formulas, a team satisfies a formula exactly when all its assignments do.
Disjunction splits a team, while existential quantification extends assignments by allowed choices; these operations explain why team semantics differs from classical semantics.
Dependence logic and existential second-order logic are equivalent for sentences, though the behavior of formulas with free variables is more delicate.
Variants add independence, inclusion, contradictory negation, modal structure, temporal traces, probabilities, or other dependencies.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dependence logic studies a central question about reasoning: what information may a choice use, and what does it determine? Its team-based framework connects formal logic with databases, imperfect-information games, belief states, computation, voting theory, and causal or counterfactual reasoning. It also illustrates that a logic’s expressive strength depends not only on its symbols, but on what counts as a situation in which a formula is true.

important_terms.definition: A logical extension of first-order logic with atoms stating that a variable is functionally determined by a tuple of variables.
An atom written conceptually as =(x1,...,xn,y), true when equal determining values always give equal y-values within a team.
A set of variable assignments used as the basic object at which formulas are evaluated.
Semantics in which formulas are evaluated relative to teams rather than individual assignments.
The usual first-order interpretation, where formulas are evaluated relative to single assignments.
The property that removing assignments from a satisfying team preserves satisfaction in dependence logic.
A game interpretation in which truth requires a uniform winning strategy under imperfect information.
The part of second-order logic allowing existential quantification over relations or functions; dependence logic has the same sentence-level expressive power as this fragment.

Why does the law of excluded middle fail for some team-semantical formulas?
How does a uniform strategy in an imperfect-information game represent functional dependence?
Should a logic’s usefulness be measured by its expressive power, its semantics, its applications, or all three?

summaries.example: A school uses a rule to assign a project level. If two students have the same math score and reading score, the rule always gives them the same level. Then the level depends on those two scores. But the level may not depend on the math score alone: two students with the same math score could receive different levels because their reading scores differ.
summaries.summary: Dependence logic is an extension of first-order logic. First-order logic already shows some dependencies through the order of its quantifiers. If we say, ‘For every student, there is a project partner,’ the partner may depend on which student we started with. But ordinary quantifier order cannot describe every pattern. Sometimes we want a choice to depend on one variable while not depending on another. Dependence logic handles this by adding dependence atoms. A dependence atom says that a value is fixed by certain other values. The atom does not merely describe where a quantifier appears; it directly describes the relationship among values. Dependence logic uses team semantics. Instead of checking a formula against one assignment, we check it against a team, which is a set of assignments. For an ordinary first-order formula, this new method agrees with the usual method: every assignment in the team must make the formula true. New rules explain how teams change during conjunction, disjunction, and quantification. Important features include locality, meaning that irrelevant variables do not affect the result, and downward closure, meaning that removing possibilities from a satisfying team keeps the formula satisfied. Dependence logic also has a game-theoretic interpretation. A player tries to prove a sentence, but a valid strategy must make dependent choices consistently: if the determining information is the same, the dependent choice must be the same. key_ideas: First-order logic uses the order of ‘for every’ and ‘there exists’ to show some dependencies.
Some useful dependency patterns do not fit that simple order.
Dependence logic adds a separate atom to state exactly what information determines what.
A team is like a list of possible situations, and team semantics checks the list as a whole.
Dependence logic can also be understood as a game where a player must make choices without using hidden information.
Related logics study independence, inclusion, beliefs, databases, and other kinds of information.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dependence logic gives us tools for describing how information controls choices. That matters in computer science, where databases contain functional dependencies; in games, where players may have incomplete information; and in philosophy, where beliefs and possible situations must be represented. Comparing dependence logic with related systems also helps us see that different meanings of ‘depends on’—such as functional determination or independence—need different formal tools.

important_terms.definition: A relationship in which some information determines another value.
A new kind of statement in dependence logic that says one variable is determined by others.
A collection of possible assignments considered together.
A method for evaluating a statement against a collection of assignments rather than one assignment.
A rule for a logical statement that is true when all relevant cases in a team satisfy it.
The feature that a smaller part of a satisfying team also satisfies the same formula in dependence logic.
